analysis.one_liner: Restores and expands workers' and students' tools to sue over discrimination, harassment, and forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: Backed by 34 House Democrats including the House Judiciary chair, the bill never received a hearing, mark-up, or vote, and died in committee when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would reverse a string of Supreme Court decisions that had narrowed civil rights enforcement. It would let people sue over policies that have a discriminatory effect even without proof of intent, let students and others recover money damages for harassment in schools and federally funded programs, ban the forced-arbitration clauses employers put in contracts, lift caps on damages for intentional job discrimination, strengthen equal-pay enforcement, let disabled air passengers sue airlines, and keep back pay available to undocumented workers who were treated unlawfully. It was referred to three House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers facing age, sex, race, or disability discrimination; service members suing state employers; students and others harassed in federally funded programs; disabled air travelers; undocumented workers denied back pay; and the plaintiffs' attorneys who bring these cases. People who signed arbitration clauses as a condition of a job would regain access to federal courts.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates a private right to challenge policies with a discriminatory effect (disparate impact) under Title VI, Title IX, the Age Discrimination Act, and the Rehabilitation Act, responding to the Supreme Court's Alexander v. Sandoval decision.

Lets victims of harassment based on race, sex, national origin, age, or disability recover damages in federally funded programs and schools, loosening the 'actual notice and deliberate indifference' standard from Gebser v. Lago Vista.

Makes arbitration clauses in employment contracts unenforceable for disputes under federal law, unless the worker agrees to arbitration after the dispute arises, so employers cannot require workers to give up court access as a hiring condition.
Repeals the caps on compensatory and punitive damages for intentional employment discrimination under the Equal Remedies Act subtitle.

Strengthens equal pay enforcement under the Fair Labor Standards Act: narrows the employer's 'factor other than sex' defense, extends coverage to applicants, removes the single-establishment limit, bars retaliation for discussing wages, adds compensatory and punitive damages, and allows class actions.

Conditions state acceptance of federal funds on waiving immunity to suits by state employees under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, USERRA, and the FLSA, restoring remedies taken away by Kimel v. Florida Board of Regents and related rulings.
Gives disabled air passengers a right to sue airlines in federal court for damages, attorney's fees, and expert fees under the Air Carrier Access Act.
Allows prevailing parties to recover expert witness fees across civil rights statutes and counts a plaintiff whose suit forced a voluntary change as a 'prevailing party' entitled to attorney's fees.
Prohibits denying back pay or other monetary relief to undocumented immigrant workers for unlawful employment practices.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, schools and universities, airlines, and state governments would bear the cost: more lawsuits, uncapped damages for intentional discrimination, harassment liability without the Gebser safe harbors, loss of forced arbitration, and expanded liability for policies with unequal effects. Arbitration providers would lose employment-dispute business.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to cases pending at enactment and to violations occurring before enactment, which critics would call retroactive change to the rules for pending disputes.

Repealing the 1991 caps on compensatory and punitive damages for intentional employment discrimination removes the ceiling Congress set in the Civil Rights Act of 1991, raising the dollar exposure of any discrimination verdict.

Expanding disparate-impact liability to federally funded programs, age discrimination, and harassment means schools, states, and employers face suit over facially neutral policies, which they argue pushes them toward defensive compliance spending and quotas by another name.

Banning pre-dispute arbitration clauses removes a faster, cheaper dispute-resolution channel that some employers and some employees deliberately choose, leaving federal court litigation as the default; the only exception is a worker agreeing to arbitration after a dispute arises.

Conditioning federal money on states waiving their 11th Amendment immunity was, by the bill's own findings, a response to recent Supreme Court federalism rulings, and its constitutional footing was contested ground.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, students, and passengers, the bill restores remedies that courts had narrowed, and most of what it does restores standards that existed before the court decisions it targets, so its benefits are concrete. The honest costs are also real: uncapped damages, broader liability for neutral policies, retroactive application to pending cases, and the loss of mandatory arbitration all raise litigation risk and compliance costs for employers, schools, and states, and some of that cost passes to taxpayers and consumers. The bill's breadth — nine titles spanning civil rights, labor, aviation, and immigration in one package — made it easy to stall and hard to move even with friendly committee chairs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees on the day it was introduced, and it never got a mark-up, hearing, or floor vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Lewis of Georgia introduced the bill on January 23, 2008, joined by 26 original co-sponsors including Reps. George Miller, John Conyers, and Eleanor Holmes Norton.

It was referred the same day to the House Judiciary, Education and Labor, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees, and within two days to the Aviation Subcommittee and the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties Subcommittee.
All 33 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on and no committee reported the bill, held a hearing, or brought it to a vote before the 110th Congress expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, schools and universities, airlines, and state governments that would have faced expanded lawsuit exposure under the bill were better off because it died in committee, as was the arbitration industry. Workers and students gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and states that avoided new liability

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat — 33 in all, no Republicans — and no floor vote ever occurred, so no record exists of how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill removes forced arbitration, lifts damages caps for intentional discrimination, narrows equal-pay defenses, and expands disparate-impact and harassment liability, all of which raise employers' exposure to worker lawsuits. Workers gain the court access employers' contracts had taken away.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and employers relying on mandatory arbitration
industries.note: Pre-dispute arbitration clauses in employment contracts would be unenforceable for federal-law claims, cutting off a lucrative dispute-resolution channel whose main effect for workers had been to route claims away from court.

Harassment damages under Title IX and Title VI would no longer require proof that officials had actual notice and were deliberately indifferent, so schools would face damages suits over harassment they failed to prevent. Students and their families gain a real remedy.
Disabled passengers would gain a direct right to sue for damages and fees under the Air Carrier Access Act, replacing enforcement left solely to an overburdened Transportation Department.
Accepting federal funds would waive state immunity to suits by state employees under the ADEA, USERRA, and the FLSA, reopening courthouse doors the Supreme Court had closed to those workers.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' bar (civil rights and employment attorneys)
industries.note: Expert-fee recovery, a broader 'prevailing party' fee definition, and expanded causes of action increase the volume and recoverability of civil rights litigation, which is also how the bill's protections get enforced for ordinary people.
